lines.en: The Song We Wrote Together
A year later, he never went back to any label.
He started his own tiny imprint and releases only what he wants. No viral collabs, no rewrites. It's not the biggest-selling thing — but every song is real.
The song that was almost sold off finally came out complete, not one word changed. Its title was a single letter: 'U.'
In the liner notes, under songwriters, there was his name — and one other.

"People keep asking who the song's about," he said one late night, curled in the little home studio that's yours now, guitar in his arms, smiling with no defenses left. "I finally tell them the truth these days."
"And what's the truth?" you asked.

He struck a chord, leaned in close, his voice that smoke-grey 3 a.m. tenderness. "…that I never wrote a single one that wasn't." The song is finished, the case stays shut, and neither of you is hiding anything.
The Version Only You Hear
He never climbed back to the top, and he didn't care.
That underground livehouse became his regular haunt. Small crowds — but every one of them truly understood him.

You never made any grand public thing of it. He's still all swagger on stage and silence off it — except with you. He still writes what he means into songs, only he's stopped flatly denying every word; and each time he finishes one, he plays it for you first, watching your face, more nervous than he ever was before an arena.
"Know the difference between the songs I release and the ones I don't?" he asked one night after closing.
"What?"

He slung the guitar onto his back, leaned in, and smiled slow and dangerous. "…the ones I don't release, I only ever play for you. And those are the good ones." The song is finished, the case stays shut, and neither of you is hiding anything.
An Unreleased Song
In the end, he never released the song, and never changed it.
He locked it away with the demos that will never see daylight, alongside every other thing he refused to admit he felt.
You two fell out of touch. He's still the untamed rockstar on stage, singing the catchy songs that sell so well, a distance in his smile that no one can cross.

Only sometimes, near the end of a show when all the lights go down, he'll suddenly stop and play, alone, a melody no one has heard — just a few bars — then slide back into the next song as if nothing happened.
No one knows what it is.

Only you do — a song never finished, never sung all the way through for anyone. It came, once, so close to being yours. The song is finished, the case stays shut, and neither of you is hiding anything.
